sections.heading: Dialogue III, Knot xvi, part 3 (printed pp. 420–424)
rows: Ereu. Vides itaque virtutem & prudentiam viam & per se causas esse voluptatis etiam corporeae; divitiarum quae ex hominum commercio & mutuis operis praestandis crescunt; amicitiarum, honorum, & potentiae. Quid amplius expectas? num ut ostendam per se causas saepius effectum sortiri & foelicius quam quae per accidens ad eadem ducunt? Unum hoc responde mihi: si quis prudens & catus ratione & tota animi sui vi ad hoc conniteretur, ut voluptatem vel potentiam securam, perpetuam, foelicem sibi faceret; Alius impetu & ferocia quadam repentina subsultim idem peteret; Utrum putes eadem caeteroqui facultate, & iisdem instrumentis munitum, desideria sibi potiori eventu coronaturum?

Ereu. You see therefore virtue and prudence to be the way and the causes by themselves [per se] of pleasure [voluptatis], even bodily [pleasure]; of riches, which grow out of the commerce [commercio] of men and out of mutual works to be rendered [praestandis]; of friendships, of honours, and of power. What more do you expect? surely not [num] that I should show that causes by themselves [per se] obtain [sortiri] their effect more often and more happily [foelicius] than those which lead to the same [things] by accident [per accidens]? This one [thing] answer me: if someone prudent and shrewd [catus] were striving [conniteretur] with reason and with the whole force of his mind toward this, that he might make for himself pleasure or power secure, perpetual, happy [foelicem]; [and] another were seeking the same by an impulse [impetu] and a certain sudden ferocity, by leaps [subsultim]; which of the two [utrum] would you think, fortified [munitum] with the same faculty in other respects [caeteroqui] and with the same instruments, will crown his desires for himself with the more powerful [potiori] outcome [eventu]?
Asphal. Nimis claret eum qui methodo & ratione uteretur; alioqui nullam vim in ratione poneremus.
Asphal. It is too clear [claret] [that it is] him who would use method and reason; otherwise we would place no force [vim] in reason.
Ereu. Iterum eum qui rationem sic applicaret, credisne passionibus deditum fore vel non?
Ereu. Again, him who would so apply reason, do you believe [him] to be going to be given over [deditum fore] to passions [passionibus], or not?
Asphal. Clarum est passionibus obnoxium esse non posse.
Asphal. It is clear [that he] cannot be liable [obnoxium] to passions.

Ereu. Asseris ergo parem harum rerum amorem, duce ratione plus effecturum quam duce passione. Quanto itaque magis rationis est quisque studiosus, tanto magis harum rerum potitur, si aequalem amorem habeat. Si vero non habet amorem quantum qui passione ducitur; meliori profecto amore praeventus est, neque impotentia his destituitur, sed quia ea non curant.

Ereu. You assert therefore [that] an equal love of these things, with reason [as] leader, will effect more than with passion [as] leader. By how much therefore each one is more studious [studiosus] of reason, by so much the more he gains possession [potitur] of these things, if he should have an equal love. But if he has not as much love as [he] who is led by passion, he has assuredly been forestalled [praeventus] by a better love, nor is he destitute of these [things] through impotence [impotentia], but because they do not care for them [ea non curant].
Asphal. Sed hoc fortassis secundum rationem ei fit, ut ea non curet: ac proinde improbis {?refercietur} hic mundus non piis.

Asphal. But this perhaps happens to him according to reason [secundum rationem], that he does not care for those [things]: and accordingly this world will be stuffed full [{?refercietur}] with the wicked [improbis], not with the pious.
[Margin, p. 422: Convenire quibusdam bonis habere bona temporalia.]
[Margin, p. 422: That it befits certain good [men] to have temporal goods.]

Ereu. Cum Dei creaturae sint de quibus petimus, bona necesse est esse, quantumvis non optima. Boni vero nihil contemnit ratio, licet meliora praeferenda doceat. Nihil itaque horum praetermittit, nisi quatenus cum meliore, cui cedat, componi non potest. Et ut sunt bonorum perpetui gradus, non aequum est ab omnibus haec contemni. A summis fortasse contemnentur, neque infimi maioris simul cum iis boni capaces erunt: sed medios esse quibus cum virtute libeant haec etiam commoda, aequum est. Unde & hoc in considerationem afferri par est. Bonos aliquos esse quibus oneri forent vel etiam exitio, si honorem vel potestatem, vel pecuniam ampliorem haberent. Non enim haec per se expetenda sunt, sed eorum fructus. Hoc est, vita longa, sana, hilaris: sive enim futurum saeculum, sive praesens respicimus, vita longa quaerenda est, ut vel melior, vel utilior. Sanam autem eam dicimus quae neque doloribus ad sese perfruendam, neque imbecillitate ab iis actionibus quae vitam suavem efficiunt, impeditur. Denique hilaritas ipsa est vitae suavitas, quam modo sectamur, dum futurae securi, huius fructum maximum ubi sit indagamus. Ex his modus voluptatum, honorum officiorum petendus est, ne imbecillitatem nimius labor parturiat, & hominem sibi eripiat: ne voluptas insalubritatem & breviorem vitam parturiat.

Ereu. Since the [things] about which we ask are creatures of God, it is necessary [that they] be good, however much [quantumvis] not the best. But reason despises nothing of good, although it teaches [that] better [things] are to be preferred. Nothing therefore of these [things] does it pass over, except inasmuch as it cannot be composed [componi] with a better [thing], to which it should yield. And as there are perpetual degrees of goods, it is not fair [aequum] [that] these [things] be despised by all. By the highest perhaps they will be despised, nor will the lowest be capable of a greater good together with them: but [that] there are middle [ones] to whom, with virtue, these advantages [commoda] also are pleasing [libeant], is fair. Whence this also it is fitting [par est] to be brought into consideration: that there are some good [men] to whom they would be for a burden or even for destruction [exitio], if they had honour or power, or more ample money. For these [things] are not to be sought by themselves [per se], but their fruit. That is, a life long, sound [sana], cheerful [hilaris]: for whether we look to the future age [saeculum] or the present, a long life is to be sought, as either better or more useful. But we call that [life] sound which is hindered neither by pains toward enjoying itself to the full [ad sese perfruendam], nor by weakness [imbecillitate] from those actions which make life sweet [suavem]. Lastly, cheerfulness [hilaritas] itself is the sweetness [suavitas] of life, which we are now pursuing [sectamur], while, secure of the future [life], we track down [indagamus] where the greatest fruit of this [life] is. From these the measure [modus] of pleasures, of honours, of offices [officiorum] is to be sought, lest excessive labour bring forth [parturiat] weakness, and snatch the man away from himself: lest pleasure bring forth unhealthiness [insalubritatem] and a shorter life.
Asphal. Cur ergo tanti viri querimonias instituerunt?
Asphal. Why then have such great men set up [instituerunt] complaints [querimonias]?

Ereu. Magni viri sub aliorum persona queruntur, sub sua querelis satisfaciunt. Unde hoc fere videbis quod brevem & fragilem impiorum esse potentiam & gloriam concludant. Quod sic se habere necessum est: Cum enim non iis quae sunt per se horum effectorum causae, nitantur; aequum est ut cito intereant & veluti herbae in solo non alto radicem mittentes, primo sole decoquantur.

Ereu. Great men complain under the person [persona] of others, under their own they satisfy the complaints [querelis]. Whence you will see this, for the most part [fere], that they conclude the power and glory of the impious to be brief and fragile. Which it is necessary to hold thus [sic se habere]: for since they rely [nitantur] not on those [things] which are by themselves [per se] the causes of these effects, it is fair [aequum] that they quickly perish, and, like grasses putting down a root in soil not deep [alto], are burnt up [decoquantur] by the first sun.

Asphal. Pulchra nobis reponis, Ereuni, & quae maturiori forte consideratione evidentiam nanciscerentur. Unum tantum super mihi difficultatem ingerit, quod si clare aperueris, Phyllida solus habeto. Postquam enim nullum a nobis fructum expectare potes, inanium certe foliorum serto, hoc est laudum nostrarum encomio te coronabimus. Est vero gemitu ferme inexplicabili dignum. Ecce enim gentem nostram quanta sit, vides, quantis terrarum spatiis, quo saeculorum ordine diffusa. Hanc ab ultimo fine suo ad quem creata est, & sine quo non esse praestaret (vanum enim illud est, quod finem propter quem natum est, non assequitur) tota sua mole deerrare, adeo ut vel nullus, vel paucissimi, & nulla prorsus ad totum genus proportione evadant beati. Si potes ad rectae gubernationis regulas adiungere; non alia posthac quaeram oracula.

Asphal. Beautiful [things] you give back [reponis] to us, Ereunius, and [things] which by a riper consideration perhaps would obtain [nanciscerentur] evidence [evidentiam]. One [thing] only remaining [super] heaps [ingerit] difficulty on me, which if you shall have clearly opened, have Phyllis alone [Phyllida solus habeto]. For since [postquam] you can expect no fruit from us, with a garland [serto] of empty leaves surely, that is, with an encomium of our praises, we shall crown you. But it is worthy of a groaning almost inexplicable [inexplicabili]. For behold, you see how great our race [gentem] is, over how great spaces of lands, in what order of ages [saeculorum] [it is] spread out; [you see] this [race] to stray away [deerrare] with its whole mass from its ultimate end, to which it was created, and without which it would be better [praestaret] not to be (for that is vain which does not attain the end for the sake of which it was born), so far that either none, or very few, and in no proportion at all to the whole kind [genus], come out [evadant] blessed [beati]. If you can join [this] to the rules of right governance [gubernationis], I shall not seek other oracles hereafter.

terms: causes by themselves [per se] / by accident [per accidens]
Scholastic-Aristotelian distinction (Phys. II.5) governing the whole Knot: virtue is the per se cause of temporal goods, so the wicked possess them only per accidens and briefly.
Archaic/poetic word (Ennius, Horace); rendered as in D3-N12.
Rare adverb (Suetonius); pictures the passionate man's irregular striving against methodical reason.
Here the pronoun (‘which of the two men’), as munitum and coronaturum are singular.
Moral sense here (the soul's passions), not the physical ‘passion’ = being acted on, as in D3-N02.
Possible theological overtone of ‘prevenient’ (gratia praeveniens): a better love has got there first.
Print reads ‘refertietur’ (or a smudged c/t); taken as future passive of refercio.
Ciceronian term for external goods (vs. honestum); White's ‘temporal goods’ of the margin.
Used repeatedly as a logical ‘it is to be expected’ as much as a moral claim.
With suavitas, White's naturalised version of the Epicurean iucunditas of part 2.
Here the ethical ‘measure’ or mean, not the metaphysical ‘mode’ of the glossary.
Used twice in the same sentence; kept the same rendering.
Rhetorical prosopopoeia: the great authors (Job, Psalmists, poets) voice complaints through characters and answer them in their own voice.
Echo of the parable of the sower (Mt 13:5–6, ‘quia non habebant altitudinem terrae … sole autem orto aestuaverunt’) and Ps 36(37):2.
‘you shall have Phyllis to yourself’ (the prize).
Virgil, Eclogue 3.107: the prize promised in the singing match to whoever solves the riddle.
with a garland [serto] of empty leaves
The poet's/victor's crown; ‘empty’ because only praise, not fruit (playing on fructus).
gens here = the human race; cf. ‘nationem hominum’ at the start of Knot XVII.
Scholastic finis ultimus (beatitudo), the theme of the next Knot.
Providential governance of the world (cf. causa gubernans in the glossary).
notes: Unit: Dialogue III, Knot xvi, part 3 of 3 (end of the Knot). PDF pp. 431–435 = printed pp. 420–424, from Ereunius' ‘Vides itaque virtutem & prudentiam viam…’ (p. 420, lower half) to the end of Asphalius' ‘…non alia posthac quaeram oracula.’ (p. 424, top). The margin ‘Nodus XVII. Cur plerique hominum a beatitudine excidant’ stands on p. 424 beside the middle of Ereunius' next speech (‘Ego vero nihil polliceor. Sed quoniam…’); following the convention used before (e.g. D3-N05/D3-N09), this Knot is ended at the preceding speaker break and Knot XVII begins with that speech. Offset +11 holds (running heads 420–424; signature Ggg iij on p. 421).

Uncertain readings: p. 421 the verb read as {?refercietur} — the print shows ‘refer[t/c]ietur’ with a damaged letter; ‘refertietur’ is not a Latin form, and the future passive of refercio (‘will be crammed’) fits the sense. p. 420 ‘praestandis’ has an ink blot over the i but is clear enough. p. 422 ‘in salubritatem’ is printed with little or no space; read as one word insalubritatem, which the sense (alongside ‘breviorem vitam’) requires. p. 421 ‘sed quia ea non curant’ — plural verb with a singular subject (the man led by reason); kept as printed, possibly a misprint for curat. p. 422 ‘honorum officiorum’ printed without a comma; kept.

Verification pass: the Latin was re-read sentence by sentence against the page images and the English. Corrections made: 4 — (a) p. 421 ‘Utrum putes … munitum … coronaturum’ first rendered ‘Do you think whether…’; corrected to the pronoun ‘which of the two’, since munitum/coronaturum are singular; (b) p. 422 ‘neque infimi maioris simul cum iis boni capaces erunt’ first rendered with maioris attached to infimi; corrected to ‘capable of a greater good’ (maioris … boni); (c) p. 422 ‘quam modo sectamur’ first rendered ‘in a measure’; corrected to the adverb ‘now’; (d) p. 423 ‘Hanc … deerrare’ first left as a loose infinitive; marked as depending on ‘vides’ with ‘[you see]’ supplied. Checked and confirmed: negatives ‘non aequum est’, ‘neque … neque … impeditur’, ‘non alto’, ‘non esse praestaret’, ‘nulla … proportione’; comparatives meliori, potiori, maturiori, breviorem, ampliorem; subjunctives conniteretur, peteret, uteretur, poneremus, forent, haberent, nanciscerentur; future perfect aperueris; future imperative habeto. Transcription matches the images.

Conventions: as in the glossary — long s, ligatures and accents normalised (œ → oe in foelicius, as printed ‘foe-’), consonantal u → v; speaker abbreviations kept (Ereu., Asphal.); supplied words in [square brackets], Latin of technical or ambiguous words in [brackets]; marginal notes placed in rows before the speech they stand beside.
